walkthroughs.body_html:
Ramadan is the 9th month of the Islamic lunar calendar.

Adult Muslims fast from dawn (Suhoor) to sunset (Iftar) — no food, drink or intimate relations.

Children, the sick, elderly, pregnant women, and travellers are exempt.

Laylat al-Qadr ('Night of Power') falls in the last 10 nights — when the Qur'an began to be revealed.

The Hajj happens once a year in Dhul Hijjah. Pilgrims wear ihram (white garments — equality before Allah).

Key rites include the Tawaf (circling the Ka'bah seven times), Sa'i (walking between Safa and Marwa), standing at Arafat, and stoning the pillars (Jamarat) at Mina.

Hajj re-enacts the actions of Ibrahim, Hajar and Isma'il.

Eid al-Fitr ('Festival of Breaking the Fast') ends Ramadan. Muslims pray together, give Zakat al-Fitr to the poor, share meals.

Eid al-Adha ('Festival of Sacrifice') happens at the end of Hajj, remembering Ibrahim's willingness to sacrifice his son. A sheep is sacrificed and shared with the poor.

Shi'a Muslims also observe Ashura — mourning the martyrdom of Husayn at Karbala (680 CE).

The Shahada is the requirement to pray five times a day.
The Trinity refers to heaven, earth and hell.
The Islamic declaration of faith: 'There is no god but Allah, and Muhammad is the messenger of Allah' — affirming monotheism and Muhammad's prophethood.
The Shahada is the Islamic pilgrimage to Mecca.
